criterion_notes.c1: Examines household drinking-water service access, intermittent/unreliable municipal piped water supply (KUKL), and reliance on informal water vendors, tankers, and public taps in the Kathmandu Valley, Nepal.
criterion_notes.c2: Passes the plain broad wording of Criterion 2 (plain_criterion2_decision = include) because the paper is framed under 'Water governance' and empirically codes residents' perceptions of municipal government incapacity, delays in the PPP-led Melamchi Water Supply Project, and corruption/mismanagement at the water utility (KUKL), alongside discussion of the 'governmentality' of resilience. However, it FAILS the active 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading of Criterion 2 (c2 = no): the study investigates psychological/phenomenological narratives of coping and social resilience in response to delayed infrastructure project delivery and general macro-governance/utility failure, rather than any specific legal, administrative, or regulatory rule-type mechanism governing service access (such as eligibility rules, tenure/documentation requirements, tariff structures, disconnection/enforcement, or regulatory rules). A single passing citation to Moench (2001) noting the absence of legal regulation over informal vendors is background context, not an empirically analysed exposure.
criterion_notes.c3: Qualitative phenomenological ('lived experiences') empirical study based on two rounds of primary interviews in Kathmandu between May and July 2016 (55 respondents overall; 36 in-depth 60-minute interviews transcribed, translated, and coded in NVivo).
criterion_notes.c4: Reports qualitative lived-experience accounts of piped water intermittency, service unavailability, reliance on public taps and private tankers, and household affordability/coping expenditures, alongside psychological perceptions of resilience.
criterion_notes.c5: Identifies population and unit of analysis (individual adult residents of Kathmandu, N=55 across two rounds / N=36 in round 2), exposure (chronic water supply shortage and delayed Melamchi Water Supply Project), outcomes (economic and emotional coping strategies, self-perceived resilience, and lack of protest), and study design (qualitative phenomenological interview study).

evidence_quotes.quote: This paper sheds light on such phenomena by constructing a fabula (or narrative structure) of the paradox by investigating the case of extreme water shortage and the coping strategies of residents in the Kathmandu Valley, Nepal.

Using a lived experiences approach, we investigate the subjective narratives of the delayed project; in particular, the self-reported perceptions of the residents’ resilience or ability to cope with adversity which engenders the self-perception of resilience, so as to identify the extent to which these two hypotheses hold true in the case of Kathmandu.
The interviews were conducted in Kathmandu from May to July 2016. A total of 55 respondents participated in the exercise.
Participants are often acutely aware of the monetary cost of obtaining bottled and tanked water when piped water supply becomes intermittent, citing figures and comparing costs with household income.

The lived experiences method has revealed how the self-perceptions of resilience is fed by a rational calculus, which is due partly to the slow and incremental nature of the problem, and a perceived ability to pay coping costs (Hero Hypothesis).

raw_response.exposure: Chronic municipal water scarcity and long-term construction delays in the Melamchi Water Supply Project (with perceived government/KUKL utility incompetence and corruption as background context)
raw_response.outcome: Household coping strategies and expenditures (purchasing tanker/bottled water, queuing at public taps), emotional/psychological coping costs, self-perceptions of social resilience, and absence of collective protest
raw_response.population_and_sample: Adult residents of Kathmandu, Nepal (individual level; N = 55 total interviewees across two rounds in May–July 2016, including N = 36 local residents in 60-minute second-round interviews)
raw_response.rationale: Exclude under E03 (Wrong exposure). While this qualitative phenomenological study empirically examines Kathmandu residents' lived experiences of intermittent piped water supply and household coping costs (satisfying c1, c3, c4, c5, and c6), its exposure and analytical focus concern psychological coping ('emotional numbing' vs. 'rational calculus') in response to physical water scarcity, delayed infrastructure project delivery (the Melamchi Water Supply Project), and broad perceptions of government/utility incompetence and corruption. Under the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 clarification, it does not examine any rule-type legal, administrative, or regulatory mechanism directly governing water service access. Under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2, it would be included due to its thematic coding of utility mismanagement, corruption, and governance perceptions.
raw_response.study_design: Qualitative phenomenological interview study (lived experiences / hermeneutical analysis using NVivo)
